title: Inguinal orchidopexy for undescended testis
subtitle: Mobilise, ligate the processus, gain length, fix in a dartos pouch

sources.org: European Association of Urology (EAU) and European Society for Paediatric Urology (ESPU)
sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology: undescended testes
Evaluation and Treatment of Cryptorchidism: AUA Guideline
Holcomb and Ashcraft's Pediatric Surgery: undescended testes and testicular tumours

indications: Palpable undescended testis (inguinal, suprascrotal or ectopic) that has not descended by 6 months of corrected age; EAU/ESPU and AUA guidance advise surgery from 6 months, completed by about 18 months at the latest.
Acquired undescended (ascending) testis in an older child, previously documented in the scrotum.
Undescended testis found at herniotomy or with a symptomatic inguinal hernia, repaired together.
contraindications: Retractile testis that can be brought to the bottom of the scrotum and stays there: no surgery, annual review for ascent.
Non-palpable testis: the open inguinal operation is not the first step; examination under anaesthesia then laparoscopy decides the plan.
Bilateral non-palpable testes, or an undescended testis with hypospadias: assess for a difference of sex development before any surgery.
Intercurrent illness; ex-premature infants need an apnoea monitoring plan rather than a cancellation.
preparation: Examine the child yourself in clinic, warm and relaxed, and document the side, the lowest position reached and the opposite testis.

Consent the parents for: wound infection and haematoma, testicular atrophy, re-ascent needing a second operation, injury to the vas or testicular vessels, a staged operation if length is insufficient, and removal of a non-viable remnant if found.

Explain that orchidopexy improves position and allows self-examination, but the risks to fertility and of later testicular cancer remain higher than in the general population, and teach testicular self-examination at puberty.
Plan day-case surgery with a caudal or ilioinguinal block agreed with the anaesthetist.
positioning: Supine, legs slightly abducted (frog-leg in an infant) so the scrotum is accessible, on a warmed mattress.
equipment: Fine paediatric set with non-toothed fine forceps, small self-retaining retractor, bipolar diathermy.
anatomy: The testis descends behind the processus vaginalis; when the processus stays patent it lies anteromedial to the cord and must be separated from it to gain length.
The gubernaculum attaches the lower pole; the vas may loop down beyond the testis within it, so the gubernaculum is divided close to the testis only after the vas is seen.
Length is limited by the testicular vessels, which are freed by retroperitoneal dissection above the internal ring; the vas usually has length to spare.
The ilioinguinal nerve lies on the cord beneath the external oblique aponeurosis.
Many palpable undescended testes lie in the superficial inguinal pouch, outside the external ring, above Scarpa fascia.
criticalSafety: Re-examine under anaesthesia: the operation depends on where the testis is now, not where it was in clinic.
Never grasp the vas or the vessels with forceps; handle the testis by the gubernaculum or tunica.
Confirm the cord is not twisted as the testis is passed into the scrotum.
Do not divide the testicular vessels in an unplanned open operation to gain length.
structuresAtRisk: Vas deferens, including a long looping vas in the gubernaculum
Inferior epigastric vessels during a Prentiss manoeuvre
Peritoneum and bowel when the processus is opened
commonErrors: Incomplete separation of the patent processus, the commonest reason the testis will not reach.
Dividing the gubernaculum blindly and cutting a looping vas.
Fixing the testis under tension, which leads to re-ascent or atrophy.
Twisting the cord when passing the testis through the scrotal tunnel.
complications: Testicular atrophy from vascular injury or tension.
Re-ascent of the testis needing redo surgery.
Injury to the vas deferens, which may only declare itself as subfertility years later.
Ilioinguinal nerve injury causing numbness or neuralgia.
postop: Day-case discharge with weight-based simple analgesia.
Avoid straddle toys and rough play for about two weeks per local advice.
Review in clinic to confirm testicular position and size, typically after several months, and teach self-examination when the child is older.

steps.emphasis: Mark the side with a parent present. Confirm whether the opposite testis is normal and what has been consented for a non-viable testis.
Today's weight for analgesia and local anaesthetic doses; gestation for any infant under the local apnoea age threshold.
Antibiotics are not routinely needed for a clean groin operation; follow local policy.
Frog-leg in an infant so the scrotum is accessible without repositioning.
Include the scrotum and both groins in the field.
Count any caudal or ilioinguinal block already given against the single maximum dose.
Bipolar diathermy near the cord; a scrotal haematoma can compress the newly placed testis.
Usually none. A non-viable remnant (nubbin) that is excised is sent for histology.
Close the external oblique aponeurosis without narrowing the ring around the cord, then Scarpa fascia, then absorbable subcuticular sutures to groin and scrotum.
Record the pre-operative position, testis size and appearance, final position, and any plan for a second stage.

step.orch.eua.title: Examination under anaesthesia confirms the plan
step.orch.eua.why: Under anaesthesia a retractile testis may come down fully, and a testis felt in clinic may become impalpable. Either finding changes the operation, and this is the last moment to change it cheaply.
how: Before preparation, examine both sides with warm hands, milking from the anterior superior iliac spine towards the scrotum.
If the testis reaches the bottom of the scrotum without tension and stays there, it is retractile: do not proceed with orchidopexy.
If the testis is now impalpable, convert to examination of the groin with laparoscopy as consented, rather than an inguinal exploration.
Record the lowest position reached and the size of both testes.
pitfalls: Operating on a retractile testis because the child is already asleep.
Exploring the groin blind for a testis that is intra-abdominal.

step.orch.access.title: Groin crease incision and finding the testis
step.orch.access.why: Many palpable undescended testes lie in the superficial inguinal pouch, outside the canal. Finding the testis before opening the aponeurosis avoids damaging a testis that was lying just under the skin.
how: Make a short incision in the lower inguinal skin crease over the internal ring.
Divide Scarpa fascia carefully and look for the testis in the superficial pouch before going deeper.
Open the external oblique aponeurosis in the line of its fibres through the external ring, identifying and protecting the ilioinguinal nerve.
structuresAtRisk: Testis in the superficial inguinal pouch
pitfalls: Cutting through Scarpa fascia boldly onto a superficially placed testis.
Dividing the ilioinguinal nerve with the aponeurosis.

step.orch.mobilise.title: Mobilising the testis and dividing the gubernaculum
step.orch.mobilise.why: The gubernaculum and cremaster tether the testis. Freeing them is easy, but the vas can loop down into the gubernaculum below the testis and be cut by an unwary division.
how: Grasp the gubernaculum or the tunica, never the testis or cord, and free the testis from its attachments.
Identify the vas before dividing the gubernaculum close to the lower pole with bipolar diathermy.
Divide the cremasteric fibres off the cord to expose the processus vaginalis.
Inspect the testis and epididymis and record size, consistency and any epididymal separation or anomaly.
structuresAtRisk: Looping vas deferens in the gubernaculum
pitfalls: Dividing the gubernaculum before seeing the vas.
Handling the testis with toothed forceps.

step.orch.processus.title: Separating and ligating the patent processus vaginalis
step.orch.processus.why: The patent processus is both a hernia sac and the main tether shortening the cord. Separating it from the vas and vessels gains most of the length needed, and its high ligation prevents a later hernia.
how: Open the processus anteriorly and identify the vas and vessels on its posterior wall.
Separate the processus from the cord structures with fine non-toothed instruments, sweeping the vas and vessels away rather than grasping them.
Continue proximally to the internal ring, twist the sac to empty it, and transfix and ligate it at the level of the extraperitoneal fat.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel or omentum within the processus
pitfalls: Tearing a thin processus and losing its proximal end.
Leaving strands of processus around the vessels that keep the cord short.

step.orch.length.title: Gaining length on the vessels
step.orch.length.why: A testis fixed under tension retracts or becomes atrophic. Length comes from freeing the vessels in the retroperitoneum, not from pulling.
how: Retract the internal ring upwards and free the lateral peritoneal bands from the testicular vessels in the retroperitoneum.
Test whether the testis reaches the bottom of the scrotum without tension.
If still short, consider moving the cord medial to the inferior epigastric vessels (Prentiss manoeuvre), dividing the vessels if necessary, so it takes a straighter course.
pitfalls: Accepting a testis that only reaches the upper scrotum under traction.
Skeletonising the vessels so their adventitial supply is lost.

step.orch.bailout.title: When the testis will not reach, or is not viable
step.orch.bailout.why: Forcing an inadequate cord into the scrotum risks losing the testis. A planned staged operation, or removal of a remnant that is not a functioning testis, are both better outcomes than an atrophic testis after a single forced attempt.
how: If length is insufficient after full mobilisation, fix the testis at the lowest point it reaches without tension and plan a second-stage operation after an interval agreed by the consultant.
If only a small remnant (nubbin) at the end of blind-ending vas and vessels is found, excise it and send it for histology.
Call the consultant before any decision to divide the testicular vessels or to remove a testis that looks viable.
Record what was found and why the plan changed, and explain it to the parents the same day.
pitfalls: Dividing the testicular vessels in an unplanned open operation.
Calling a small but viable testis a nubbin and removing it.

step.orch.dartos-pouch.title: Placing the testis in a subdartos pouch
step.orch.dartos-pouch.why: A pouch between the scrotal skin and the dartos holds the testis in the scrotum without sutures through it. The commonest technical cause of a lost testis at this stage is a twisted cord.
how: Make a transverse incision in the scrotal skin and develop a pouch between skin and dartos with blunt dissection.
Pass a clamp up through the dartos into the groin and draw the testis down by the gubernaculum remnant, keeping the cord in its natural orientation.
Confirm the cord is not twisted, with the epididymis posterior and the vessels running straight.
Narrow the dartos opening around the cord to hold the testis, avoiding sutures through the testicular parenchyma, then close the scrotal skin.
pitfalls: Twisting the cord as the testis is pulled through.
Narrowing the dartos neck so tightly that it constricts the vessels.
